newsitem.title: USA: China 1997/8 cotton imports 650,000 Ts--USDA aide.
newsitem.headline: China 1997/8 cotton imports 650,000 Ts--USDA aide.

text.p: China is forecast to import 650,000 tonnes of cotton in 1997/98 (August-July), unchanged from a newly increased estimate for 1996/97, the U.S. Agriculture Department attache in Beijing said.

In a May 31 report released Thursday, the attache said China should remain a major cotton importer for the foreseeable future and noted that China's agricultural statistical agency appears to have greatly overestimated past production.
Recently, the State Statistical Bureau pegged 1996 Chinese cotton production at 4.2 million tonnes, the attache said.

But "based on travel, numerous discussion with Chinese officials, media reports and trade contacts," the USDA office in Beijing "estimates that 1996 cotton production did not exceed 3.6 million tonnes," the attache said.
Similarly, the attache put the 1995 cotton crop at less than 4.3 million tonnes, compared to the SSB's estimate of more than 4.7 million.

"The decline in China's cotton production is the result of several factors, including pressure to grow more food grains rather than fibers; the rising costs of producing cotton, making it less attractive to farmers; continued problems with bollworm; and state controls and pricing policies, which discourage farmers," the attache said.

"No one know how far China's cotton production will decline. It seems clear that, at least in the short run, China is unlikely to be a major cotton exporter and will continue to import large volumes of cotton," the attache said.

The attache pegged China's 1997 cotton crop at 3.6 million tonnes. The Chinese government has not made an official forecast, but government officials have been quoted saying acreage would be down five to 10 percent, the attache said.
China's cotton imports should remain high, despite the SSB's tendency to greatly overstate the size of the crops. However, there some clouds on the horizon, the attache said.
"First, China's yarn and fabric imports increased again in 1996, raising doubts about further growth in raw cotton demand in China," the attache said.

"Second, the U.S. share of the China cotton import market has fallen sharply in the past nine months, so that even as China's total cotton imports begin climbing again, the share of these imports from the United States is falling."
U.S. exporters would be wise to pay more attention to Chinese concerns about short fibre content and excessive contamination in shipments of U.S. cotton, the attache said.
